overview.summary: Learn to turn raw business data into decisions with spreadsheets, SQL, Python, dashboards and AI assistants, and to check what the AI produces. Ten practical modules use free tools and one practice dataset from Masala Mart, a fictional Indian spice brand. Then a final assessment, and a portfolio project with a mentor.
overview.audience: students and graduates who want an entry-level data analyst role, or to use data well in any job
outcomes: Turn a vague business question into an analysis plan with a clear decision
Clean, combine and summarise data in spreadsheets, SQL and Python (pandas)
Tell a real change from noise using spread, samples and simple A/B tests
Build a dashboard that tracks what matters and flags problems early
Use AI assistants to work faster, and check everything they produce
Present a recommendation a manager can act on, backed by a portfolio project

items.statement: Before I answer a question with numbers, I check exactly what is being asked.
I notice when a statistic in the news or on social media doesn’t add up.
I take the numbers in reports at face value.
I use formulas instead of working things out by hand.
I sort or filter a spreadsheet to find the rows I need, instead of scrolling through it.
Spreadsheets with more than a few hundred rows overwhelm me.
I spot typos, duplicates and inconsistent entries in lists.
I keep a copy of the original file before I change any data.
I start working with data without checking it first.
When I need one number from a long list, I write down the steps (which rows, which groups, which total) before I start.
I look up the exact syntax of a formula or command instead of guessing it.
When I need figures from a large table, I ask someone else to pull them for me.
I ask how many people a survey asked before I trust its result.
When I see an average, I look at the highest and lowest values behind it.
When two things happen together, I assume one causes the other.
When I repeat the same steps on a file every week, I look for a way to automate them.
When a tool shows an error, I read it and try to fix it myself.
I avoid tasks that involve typing commands or code.
I choose charts that make the main point obvious.
I notice when a chart’s design exaggerates a difference.
I add as many charts as I can to show I’ve been thorough.
I use AI tools to speed up my studies or work.
I check an AI tool’s answer against another source before relying on it.
If an AI tool sounds confident, I trust its answer.
I can explain a complicated finding in two or three sentences.
I start a presentation with my main point.
I find it hard to say what my analysis means for a decision.

modules.title: Thinking like an analyst
modules.summary: Turn vague questions into answerable ones, know your data types, and read numbers critically.
modules.outcome: Turn a vague business question into a specific one you can answer with data.

learn.title: Start with the decision, not the data
learn.body:
An analysis is useful only if it changes a decision. So before you open a spreadsheet, answer four questions. Who will decide? What will they decide? What measure would change their mind? Over what period?

Worked example. Meera owns a bakery in Pune. She asks, “How are sales doing?”
- Who decides: Meera.
- The decision: whether to keep the ₹50-off Diwali offer next week.
- The measure: orders a day, and money earned after the discount.
- The period: the 10 days of the offer against the 10 days before it.

Her question becomes: “Did the ₹50 offer bring enough extra orders to cover the discount?” It has an owner, a deadline and an action.

The common mistake is to start pulling every number you can find. You end up with a long report and no answer.

learn.title: Know your data types
learn.body:
Every column has a type, and the type decides what you can do with it.
- Numbers you can add: order value in ₹, quantity, minutes.
- Numbers and codes that are really labels: order ID, product code (SKU), phone number, PIN code.
- Categories: city, payment method. You count and group them.
- Dates: you sort them and group them by month.
- Free text: a customer’s comment.

Worked example. An orders file has six columns: order_id, pin_code, order_date, city, payment_method and order_value. Only order_value should be added up. Average the pin_code column and you get a number like 411037. It looks precise and means nothing.

Watch for numbers and dates stored as text. “₹1,250” typed with the ₹ sign can be stored as text, and a SUM skips text. A date stored as text, such as 05/04/2026, sorts like a word, not like a date.

learn.title: Read numbers critically
learn.body:
An average can hide what is going on. An average order of ₹850 could mean most orders are near ₹850. Or it could mean most are ₹300 and a few bulk orders are ₹20,000. So look at the spread too: the minimum, the maximum and the median (the middle value when you sort them).

Next, two numbers moving together does not prove that one causes the other. Worked example: at a coaching centre in Kota, students who attend doubt-clearing sessions score 15% higher. Does attending cause it? Maybe keen students attend, and also study more at home. Both could share a cause.

Only a fair comparison shows cause. One example is a test where students are picked at random to attend. You will learn to design one in the statistics module.

tasks.title: Sharpen a vague question
tasks.prompt: A café chain’s owner in Hyderabad asks: “Why are we losing customers?” Rewrite this as two or three specific questions you could answer with data. For each one, write the four parts from the first card: who decides, the decision, the measure and the period. Then say what data you would need.
tasks.hint: Say what “losing” looks like in the data, for example no visit in 60 days. Name which customers you mean: regulars, new ones, or one branch.

tasks.title: Spot the wrong type
tasks.prompt: You will analyse Masala Mart, a fictional online spice brand. Its raw orders file has nine columns: order_id, order_date, customer_id, city, sku, quantity, order_value, payment_method, returned. Three of its rows: [Row 1] MM10002 | 01/10/2025 | C0009 | Kochi | MM-BL-03 | 1 | ₹150 | UPI | 0 [Row 2] MM10004 | 01/10/2025 | C0117 | bengaluru | MM-GS-03 | 4 | ₹380 | UPI | 0 [Row 3] MM10001 | 01/10/2025 | C0035 | Hyderabad | MM-BL-02 | 4 | 520 | COD | 0. Now: label each column’s type. Which two columns would break a total or a sort, and how? Name one other problem. “returned” is 1 if returned, 0 if kept: what would its average tell you?
tasks.hint: Would a SUM count “₹150”? Stored as text, would 01/10/2025 sort before or after 02/09/2025? Look at how each city is typed.

reflection.prompt: Think of a decision you made recently: a phone, a course, a trip. What data did you use, and what data do you wish you had?
reflection.hint: Small personal decisions use the same habits as business ones.

quiz.title: The report by Friday

context.background: The founder says weekly orders “feel slower” and wants a report by Friday.
context.objective: Make the request answerable and useful.
context.information: 18 months of orders with date, city, basket value and customer ID.

quiz.question: What is the best first step?
options: Agree with the founder which decision the report is for and how “slower” will be measured
Build a dashboard of every metric the order data lets you calculate, then look for what changed
Compare this week’s orders with last week’s, city by city, and send the founder the result
Ask the tech team for every table they have, so nothing is missing when you start
quiz.explanation: Agreeing on the decision and the measure makes the work answerable and useful. For example, compare orders per week for the last 8 weeks with the same weeks last year.
quiz.why_wrong: A dashboard of everything answers nothing in particular; one week against the last is noisy (festivals, salary days); asking for more data delays the work without knowing what is needed.
quiz.learning_outcome: Frame the question before touching the data.

quiz.title: The delivery app’s customer table
quiz.scenario: A grocery delivery app in Guwahati exports its customer table. An intern adds a row of averages under every column that holds numbers.
quiz.question: Which column’s average will mean nothing?
options: Store code (such as 1043)
Delivery time in minutes
Order value in ₹ (such as 450)
Items per order
quiz.explanation: A store code is a label written in digits: 1043 names a store and measures nothing. Its average is a number that matches no store and means nothing.
quiz.why_wrong: Delivery time in minutes is a real quantity, so its average (or median) is meaningful; order value in ₹ is an amount you can add and average; items per order is a count, and its average shows the typical basket size.
quiz.learning_outcome: Check a column’s type before you summarise it.

quiz.title: Fees at a study centre
quiz.scenario: A study centre records monthly fees for 50 students. 47 pay between ₹2,000 and ₹2,500; three corporate-sponsored students pay ₹30,000 each.
quiz.question: Which single number best describes what a typical student pays?
options: The mean (average) fee
The highest fee
The midpoint of the lowest and highest fees
The median fee
quiz.explanation: The three ₹30,000 fees pull the mean up to between ₹3,680 and ₹4,150, above what 47 of the 50 students pay. The median stays at what the middle student pays, between ₹2,000 and ₹2,500.
quiz.why_wrong: The mean is pulled up by the three ₹30,000 fees; the highest fee describes the exception, not the typical student; the midpoint of the lowest and highest fees, about ₹16,000, is set by the two extremes.
quiz.learning_outcome: Use the median when a few extreme values distort the mean.

quiz.title: Dark mode and test scores
quiz.scenario: A coaching app finds that students who switch on dark mode score 12% higher in its tests. The product manager wants to make dark mode the default to raise scores.
quiz.question: What is the soundest response?
options: Agree, because a 12% difference across thousands of students is far too large to be a coincidence
Reject it, because a 12% rise is too small to justify changing the app’s default
Agree, but switch it on first for the lowest scorers, since they have the most to gain
Say dark-mode users may differ in other ways (more engaged, studying late), so test it first
quiz.explanation: Keen, heavy users may be the ones who pick dark mode, and they would score higher anyway. Only a fair test, where some new users get dark mode by chance, shows whether the setting itself changes scores.
quiz.why_wrong: A large gap can still come from who chooses dark mode rather than from the setting; 12% would matter if the setting really caused it; switching it on for low scorers still assumes the setting causes the scores.
quiz.learning_outcome: Two things moving together doesn’t mean one causes the other.

modules.title: Spreadsheets that answer questions
modules.summary: Tables, fixed references, XLOOKUP, SUMIFS and pivot tables: answer business questions in Google Sheets or Excel.
modules.outcome: Answer a business question, such as a return rate by payment method, with lookups, SUMIFS and pivot tables in a spreadsheet.

learn.title: Set up the sheet: tables and fixed references
learn.body:
Start with a clean layout: one header row, one row per record, no blank rows and no merged cells. Then turn the range into a table. In Google Sheets, use Format > Convert to table. In Excel, press Ctrl+T. A table grows with new rows, so formulas and pivot tables keep working.

Next, fixed references. Worked example: the GST rate, 18%, is in cell F1. Prices are in column B. In C2 you write:
=B2*$F$1
Then you fill it down the column. B2 becomes B3, B4 and so on, but $F$1 stays fixed. The $ before F fixes the column, and the $ before 1 fixes the row.

The common mistake is writing =B2*F1. Filled down, row 3 becomes =B3*F2. F2 is empty, so every result after row 2 shows 0.

learn.title: Look things up with XLOOKUP
learn.body:
XLOOKUP finds a value in one column and returns the matching value from another. Worked example: a stationery shop’s Prices tab lists codes in column A and categories in column B. P-101 is Pens, N-202 is Notebooks and F-303 is Files. An order in A2 has the code N-202.
=XLOOKUP(A2, Prices!A:A, Prices!B:B, "Not found")
In order: what to find, where to look, what to bring back, and what to show if it is missing. The result is Notebooks. For a code like X-999, it shows Not found.

XLOOKUP works in Google Sheets and in Excel 2021 or later. It isn’t in Excel 2016 or 2019. There, use =VLOOKUP(A2, Prices!A:B, 2, FALSE).

Common mistakes: leaving VLOOKUP’s last argument out, or setting it to TRUE. That asks for an approximate match, which can quietly return the wrong row. Also, “N-202 ” with a trailing space won’t match “N-202”.

learn.title: Summarise with a pivot table or SUMIFS
learn.body:
A pivot table groups and totals thousands of rows in seconds. In Google Sheets, use Insert > Pivot table; in Excel, Insert > PivotTable. Choose Rows and Values, then set each value to Sum, Count or Average.

Worked example: a Surat saree store wants its return rate by payment method. Its Returned column holds 1 for returned and 0 for kept. Put payment method in Rows. Put Returned in Values as Average. The average of 1s and 0s is the share returned: Card 4%, UPI 7%, cash on delivery (COD) 19%.

Common mistake: showing Returned as “Sum, % of column total”. That gives each method’s share of all returns, not its return rate.

SUMIFS answers the same kind of question with a formula. =SUMIFS(F:F, C:C, "COD") adds column F where column C is COD. COUNTIFS counts rows the same way, so the COD return rate is:
=SUMIFS(F:F, C:C, "COD")/COUNTIFS(C:C, "COD")

tasks.title: Return rate by payment method
tasks.prompt: Open a blank Google Sheet, in the app or a browser. In cell A1, type =IMPORTDATA("https://myskills.org.in/practice-data/masala-mart/orders.csv") to load Masala Mart’s 2,030 orders from October 2025 to September 2026. (Or download the file and use File > Import.) Build a pivot table: payment_method in Rows, returned in Values as Average. Report the return rate for UPI, Card and COD, to one decimal place. Then check the COD rate with a formula: =SUMIFS(I:I, H:H, "COD")/COUNTIFS(H:H, "COD").
tasks.hint: Check yourself: all three rates are under 20%. If one is over 50%, you showed a share of all returns, not a rate. The pivot and the formula must agree.

tasks.title: Bring in the category
tasks.prompt: Add a second tab to the same Google Sheet and name it products. In its cell A1, type =IMPORTDATA("https://myskills.org.in/practice-data/masala-mart/products.csv"). Back in the orders tab, write an XLOOKUP in J2 that brings in each order’s category from the products tab. It should show "Not found" when the SKU is missing. Fill it down every row. Report how many rows show Not found, and which SKUs they are. Then find revenue by category with a pivot table or SUMIFS.
tasks.hint: The SKU is in column E of orders, and in columns A (SKU) and C (category) of products. To fill down on a phone, copy J2, select the column below it and paste. Count the misses with =COUNTIF(J:J, "Not found").

reflection.prompt: What is one spreadsheet task you do, or have seen done, by hand that a table, a lookup or a PivotTable could do in seconds?
reflection.hint: Copying totals from one sheet to another counts.

quiz.title: The rows the pivot table misses
quiz.scenario: Every Monday, a Vadodara electronics shop pastes last week’s sales under the old rows of its Google Sheet. Its pivot table and its total formulas keep leaving out the new rows.
quiz.question: Which change fixes this for good?
options: Sort the sheet by date each Monday, so that the newest rows are at the top
Paste each week into a new tab, so the old rows can never be changed by mistake
Leave a blank row between weeks, so each week’s sales are easy to find
Convert the range to a table, so formulas and the pivot table include new rows
quiz.explanation: A table grows as rows are added. So everything built on it, pivot tables and formulas alike, picks up each new week without being edited.
quiz.why_wrong: Sorting changes the order of the rows, not the range the pivot table reads; a new tab each week splits the data, so the pivot table and totals cover even less of it; blank rows break the one-block layout that tables and pivot tables need.
quiz.learning_outcome: Turn data into a table so new rows are included automatically.

quiz.title: Invoices and a product master
quiz.scenario: A distributor in Ludhiana is matching 4,000 invoice lines to a 900-row product master. Some SKUs on the invoices are new and not yet in the master.
quiz.question: Which formula returns the product category, and shows “New SKU” when there is no match?
options: =IFERROR(VLOOKUP(B2, Master, 2, TRUE), "New SKU")
=XLOOKUP(Master[SKU], B2, Master[Category], "New SKU")
=IFNA(SUMIF(Master[SKU], B2, Master[Category]), "New SKU")
=XLOOKUP(B2, Master[SKU], Master[Category], "New SKU")
quiz.explanation: XLOOKUP takes what to find (B2), where to look (Master[SKU]), what to bring back (Master[Category]) and what to show if it is missing. Its default is an exact match, so a new SKU gets “New SKU”, not a wrong category.
quiz.why_wrong: VLOOKUP with TRUE does an approximate match, so it can quietly return the wrong category instead of “New SKU”; XLOOKUP(Master[SKU], B2, …) has the value to find and the place to look swapped; SUMIF adds numbers and can’t return a text category.
quiz.learning_outcome: Use an exact-match lookup with a clear “not found” value.

quiz.title: Trial classes that turn into members
quiz.scenario: A gym in Dehradun logs every free trial class in a sheet. Its Joined column holds 1 if the person then bought a membership and 0 if not. Source (Instagram, walk-in or referral) is in the Rows of a pivot table.
quiz.question: Which Values setting shows each source’s joining rate directly?
options: Sum of Joined, shown as % of column total
Count of Joined
Average of Joined
Max of Joined
quiz.explanation: The average of a column of 1s and 0s is the share of 1s. So the average of Joined for each source is the share of that source’s trial visitors who joined.
quiz.why_wrong: Sum of Joined as % of column total gives each source’s share of all new members, not its own joining rate; Count of Joined counts every trial, 1s and 0s alike; Max of Joined shows 1 as soon as one person from that source joins.
quiz.learning_outcome: Averaging a 1/0 column gives a rate.

quiz.title: Commission on every row
quiz.scenario: A Belagavi electronics shop keeps each sale’s amount in column B and its 3% commission rate in cell H1. You want the commission in C2, and then you will fill the formula down to C400.
quiz.question: What should C2 contain?
quiz.explanation: Filled down, B2 must move to B3, B4 and so on, but every row must use the rate in H1. $H$1 fixes both the column and the row, so the rate stays put.
quiz.why_wrong: $B$2 fixes the amount instead, so every row uses the first sale while H1 slides down to empty cells; $H1 fixes only the column, so row 3 reads H2, which is empty; $B2 fixes the amount’s column, but the rate still slides down to H2.
quiz.learning_outcome: Fix a shared value with $ on both its column and its row.

modules.title: Cleaning messy data
modules.summary: Profile data, fix duplicates, dates, text amounts and inconsistent categories, and handle blanks honestly.
modules.outcome: Clean a messy sales export so its row count and totals can be trusted, with a log of every fix.

learn.title: Profile before you clean
learn.body:
Profiling means measuring the data before you change it. Count the rows. Then, for each column, count the blanks and the different values, and look at the smallest and largest values.

Worked example: a Jaipur coaching centre’s enquiry list has 1,200 rows. Profiling shows:
- city: 14 different values for 6 real cities (“Jaipur”, “jaipur”, “JAIPUR ”).
- age: smallest 0, largest 212. Both are typing errors.
- enquiry_date: some as 03/04/2026, some as 2026-04-03.
- 37 rows appear twice.
Now you have a list of what to fix, and a way to measure each fix.

Free tools in Google Sheets: =COUNTA(A:A) counts filled cells, and =COUNTUNIQUE(D:D) counts different values. Data > Column stats profiles one column. A pivot table of a column shows every spelling in it.

learn.title: Fix the cause, and keep a log
learn.body:
Keep the raw file untouched and clean a copy. Fix one problem at a time and write each step down.

Worked example, continuing the enquiry list:
Step 1: removed exact duplicate rows (Data > Data cleanup > Remove duplicates). 1,200 → 1,163 rows.
Step 2: trimmed spaces in city (Data > Data cleanup > Trim whitespace). 41 cells changed.
Step 3: mapped “jaipur” and “JAIPUR” to “Jaipur” with a two-column mapping tab and XLOOKUP. 212 rows.
Step 4: set age to blank where it was 0 or over 100. 9 rows.

Each line says what changed and how many rows. Anyone can repeat your work, and a manager can trust the totals. In Excel, Power Query records the same steps so you can rerun them next month.

The common mistake is cleaning silently. If the totals change and nobody knows why, nobody trusts them.

learn.title: Missing is not zero
learn.body:
A blank is unknown, not zero. Decide column by column. You can leave it out, fill it from another source, or flag it. Then say how many rows your choice affects.

Worked example: a Kochi food delivery app logs 100 deliveries. 6 have no delivery time, and the riders say all 6 were very late. The 94 recorded deliveries average 28 minutes. If the 6 took about 80 minutes each, the true average is about 31 minutes. Typing 0 into the blanks gives 26 minutes.

So leaving the blanks out makes deliveries look a little faster than they are. Filling them with 0 makes it worse.

Always ask: are the missing rows different from the rest? If the slow deliveries are the ones missing, say so beside your number.

tasks.title: Clean Masala Mart’s raw export
tasks.prompt: Open a blank Google Sheet and type in A1: =IMPORTDATA("https://myskills.org.in/practice-data/masala-mart/orders_raw.csv"). Copy everything, then paste it into a new tab with Edit > Paste special > Values only, so you can edit it. Profile it, then clean it. Remove duplicate rows and make the city names consistent. Make sure order_value is a number and order_date is read as day/month/year. Fill blank cities from customers.csv (https://myskills.org.in/practice-data/masala-mart/customers.csv) with XLOOKUP on customer_id. Submit your cleaning log with a row count for each step, and your final row count and total order value.
tasks.hint: Check yourself against the clean file orders.csv: you should end with 10 cities and the same row count and total. For order_value, type =ISNUMBER(G3) next to the “₹150” cell. With the India locale, Sheets may already read ₹150 as a number, so you get TRUE: nothing to fix. If you get FALSE, it is text: use =VALUE(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(G3,"₹",""),",","")) in a new column. You will meet the text version again in Module 7, Python and pandas for analysis. For dates, look at File > Settings > Locale. With India, 01/10/2025 is read as 1 October; with United States, it can be read as 10 January.

tasks.title: Decide about blanks
tasks.prompt: A Lucknow pharmacy’s delivery sheet has 50 deliveries. 45 have a delivery time, and they average 40 minutes. 5 are blank, and the delivery staff say those 5 took about 90 minutes each because of a road closure. Work out the average three ways: leaving the blanks out, filling them with 0, and using the staff’s estimate. Say which number you would report, and write the one-line note you would put beside it.
tasks.hint: Average = total minutes ÷ number of deliveries counted. Start with the total for the 45: 45 × 40.

reflection.prompt: What is the messiest data you have seen: a form, a contact list, an attendance register? What would you fix first, and why?
reflection.hint: Think about which problem would cause the biggest wrong answer.

quiz.title: Bookings and payments
quiz.scenario: An event-ticketing startup’s bookings export has 5,200 rows, but the payments team counts 5,000 payments. 200 booking IDs appear twice, and each pair is identical in every column.
quiz.question: What is the right action?
options: Delete all 400 rows that share a booking ID, since you can’t tell which copy is real
Remove the 200 exact duplicates, keeping one copy of each, and note it in the cleaning log
Keep every row, because removing data could hide bookings the payments team missed
Merge each pair by averaging their values, so nothing from either row is lost
quiz.explanation: Identical rows with the same ID are true duplicates: keep one of each and record the change so the numbers can be reconciled.
quiz.why_wrong: Deleting both copies loses 200 real bookings; keeping them double-counts; averaging identical rows changes nothing and hides the problem.
quiz.learning_outcome: Remove true duplicates, keep one copy, and log it.

quiz.title: The courier’s dates
quiz.scenario: A Bhubaneswar courier company exports its booking dates as text. The first three read 04/05/2026, 13/05/2026 and 28/02/2026.
quiz.question: What format are the dates in?
options: Month/day/year
Year/month/day
Day/month/year
It can’t be worked out from these values
quiz.explanation: 13 and 28 can’t be months, so the first number must be the day. That makes 04/05/2026 4 May 2026, not 5 April.
quiz.why_wrong: In month/day/year no first number could be above 12, but 13 and 28 are; year/month/day would start with a four-digit year, not end with one; the values above 12 settle it, so it can be worked out.
quiz.learning_outcome: Use impossible values to work out an ambiguous date format.

quiz.title: One city, four spellings
quiz.scenario: A salon chain’s booking export has a city column. Profiling shows “Bengaluru”, “Bangalore”, “bangalore ” and “BLR”, all for the same city.
quiz.question: What is the most reliable fix?
options: Delete the rows that don’t say “Bengaluru”, since they were entered incorrectly
Leave them as they are, because a pivot table groups similar spellings together
Use Find and Replace on “Bangalore”, the most common variant, and leave the rest as they are
Trim spaces, map every variant to one name in a lookup table, then check nothing is left
quiz.explanation: Trimming removes stray spaces, and a mapping table turns every variant into one name the same way each time. The final check, such as a pivot table of the column, catches any spelling the map missed.
quiz.why_wrong: Deleting rows loses real bookings; a pivot table doesn’t merge different spellings such as Bengaluru, Bangalore and BLR; one Find and Replace misses the other variants and the trailing space.
quiz.learning_outcome: Standardise categories with a mapping, then verify.

quiz.title: The patients who left
quiz.scenario: A Vellore hospital’s outpatient log records when each patient arrived and when a doctor saw them. 9% of rows have no “seen at” time. Most are patients who left after a long wait without being seen.
quiz.question: If you drop those rows, how does the average waiting time you report compare with what patients actually experienced?
options: It matches, because rows with no “seen at” time would be left out of the average anyway
It looks better than reality, because the longest waits are the ones left out
It looks worse than reality, because the patients who left had the longest waits
It can’t be compared at all, so no waiting-time figure should be reported
quiz.explanation: The missing rows aren’t random: they are mostly the patients who waited longest. Leaving them out makes waiting look shorter than patients found it, so report the average with a note on how many left unseen.
quiz.why_wrong: Dropping the rows or letting the average skip them leaves out the longest waits, so the figure isn’t what patients went through; leaving out the longest waits makes the average shorter, not longer; the average can still be reported if you say what it leaves out.
quiz.learning_outcome: Ask why data is missing before you drop it.

modules.title: SQL foundations: asking a database questions
modules.summary: SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING and NULLs: filter, group and summarise data in a free database in your browser.
modules.outcome: Write and run SELECT queries that filter, group and summarise a table, and handle blanks (NULL) correctly.

learn.title: One question, one query
learn.body:
SQL reads almost like a sentence: SELECT the columns, FROM a table, WHERE rows match, ORDER BY a column. Worked example: a payments table has 5 rows.
payment_id | city | amount
1 | Pune | 400
2 | Indore | 1200
3 | Pune | 900
4 | Nagpur | 250
5 | Pune | 650

SELECT payment_id, amount
FROM payments
WHERE city = 'Pune' AND amount > 500
ORDER BY amount DESC;
Result: 2 rows. Payment 3 (900), then payment 5 (650). Text goes in single quotes; numbers don’t.

Run SQL free in the DuckDB shell at shell.duckdb.org. It works in any browser, phone included, and the queries run on your device. Load a CSV file with one line:
CREATE TABLE orders AS SELECT * FROM 'https://myskills.org.in/practice-data/masala-mart/orders.csv';
The table lasts until you close the tab.

learn.title: GROUP BY turns rows into answers
learn.body:
COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX summarise rows. GROUP BY decides the groups. With the same 5 payments:
SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS payments, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM payments
GROUP BY city;
Result: Pune 3 payments, 1950. Indore 1, 1200. Nagpur 1, 250.
Every column in SELECT must be in the GROUP BY or inside a summary function.

Common mistake with dates. Say paid_at holds a date and a time. This misses almost all of 30 April:
WHERE paid_at BETWEEN '2026-04-01' AND '2026-04-30'
'2026-04-30' means midnight at the start of 30 April. Write a half-open range instead:
WHERE paid_at >= '2026-04-01' AND paid_at < '2026-05-01'
It works for dates with or without times.

learn.title: WHERE, HAVING and NULL
learn.body:
WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after it. A query runs in this order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY.

A blank in a database is NULL, meaning unknown. Test it with IS NULL or IS NOT NULL. Writing = NULL never finds a row, because nothing equals unknown.

AVG, SUM and COUNT(column) skip NULLs. COUNT(*) counts every row. Worked example: four reviews of a Chennai café.
review_id | stars
1 | 5
2 | NULL
3 | 3
4 | NULL
COUNT(*) is 4. COUNT(stars) is 2. AVG(stars) is 4.0: the average of the 2 rated reviews, not (5 + 3) ÷ 4.
To list the unrated reviews:
SELECT review_id FROM reviews WHERE stars IS NULL;

tasks.title: Orders by payment method in April
tasks.prompt: Open shell.duckdb.org and load Masala Mart’s orders with the CREATE TABLE line from the first card. The table has order_id, order_date, customer_id, city, sku, quantity, order_value, payment_method and returned. Write and run a query that shows, for each payment_method, the number of orders and the total order_value in April 2026, largest total first. Paste your query and its result.
tasks.hint: Use the half-open date range from the second card. Check yourself: your three order counts should add up to 165, the number of April orders.

tasks.title: Run it, then explain it
tasks.prompt: Run this query on the same table: SELECT city, AVG(order_value) AS avg_value FROM orders WHERE returned = 0 GROUP BY city HAVING COUNT(*) >= 100 ORDER BY avg_value DESC; Then explain in plain words, for a manager who doesn’t know SQL, what it returns. How many cities are in the result, and why are the others missing?
tasks.hint: Write a second query that counts each city’s kept orders (returned = 0). Which cities have fewer than 100? Why might a manager want them left out?

reflection.prompt: Which questions at a business you know could be answered with a single GROUP BY query? Write two.
reflection.hint: Think “for each …, how many / how much …?”

quiz.title: Orders in each city
quiz.scenario: A Jamshedpur hardware chain keeps its sales in a table orders(order_id, city, order_value).
quiz.question: Which query counts the orders in each city?
options: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT city) FROM orders;
SELECT city, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY city;
SELECT city, COUNT(*) FROM orders ORDER BY city;
SELECT city, SUM(order_id) FROM orders GROUP BY city;
quiz.explanation: GROUP BY city makes one group per city, and COUNT(*) counts the rows in each.
quiz.why_wrong: COUNT(DISTINCT city) gives one number, how many cities there are; without GROUP BY, mixing city and COUNT(*) is an error in most databases, and ORDER BY only sorts; adding up order IDs gives a meaningless total.
quiz.learning_outcome: GROUP BY plus a summary function answers “for each …”.

quiz.title: Cities above ₹10 lakh
quiz.scenario: A Lucknow sweet-shop chain has a table orders(order_id, city, order_value). The owner wants the cities whose total revenue is above ₹10 lakh.
quiz.question: Which clause filters on that total?
options: WHERE SUM(order_value) > 1000000
HAVING SUM(order_value) > 1000000
ORDER BY SUM(order_value) > 1000000
GROUP BY SUM(order_value) > 1000000
quiz.explanation: WHERE filters rows before they are grouped, so the city totals don’t exist yet. HAVING filters after GROUP BY, so it can test SUM(order_value) > 1000000 (₹10 lakh).
quiz.why_wrong: WHERE runs before grouping, so SUM(order_value) can’t be used there and the query fails; ORDER BY sorts the result but removes nothing; GROUP BY sets the groups and can’t filter them.
quiz.learning_outcome: Filter groups with HAVING, rows with WHERE.

quiz.title: Leads without a phone number
quiz.scenario: A Kolkata property agency runs SELECT COUNT(*) FROM leads WHERE phone = NULL; and gets 0, though many leads have no phone number.
quiz.question: Why does it return 0?
options: The table has no leads with a missing phone number, so 0 is right
“= NULL” is never true; it should be WHERE phone IS NULL
COUNT(*) skips rows where any of the columns is NULL
NULL needs quotes, as in WHERE phone = 'NULL'
quiz.explanation: NULL means unknown, and nothing equals unknown, so “phone = NULL” is never true and no row passes. WHERE phone IS NULL finds the blanks.
quiz.why_wrong: The leads do have missing phones; COUNT(*) counts rows whatever their values; 'NULL' in quotes is just the text NULL.
quiz.learning_outcome: Test for missing values with IS NULL.

quiz.title: Rides with no rating
quiz.scenario: A Patna cab app’s table rides(ride_id, rating) has 1,000 rides. 400 riders gave no rating, so their rating is NULL. SELECT AVG(rating) FROM rides; returns 4.2.
quiz.question: What does 4.2 describe?
options: The total of all ratings divided by all 1,000 rides
The middle rating of the 600 rated rides, since AVG skips the NULLs
The average of the 600 rides that have a rating
Nothing useful, because the NULLs make AVG return an error
quiz.explanation: AVG, like SUM and COUNT(rating), skips NULLs; only COUNT(*) counts every row. So 4.2 is the average of the 600 rated rides. A report should say “4.2 stars from the 60% of rides that were rated”.
quiz.why_wrong: Dividing by all 1,000 rides would treat the 400 missing ratings as 0 and give a much lower number; AVG is a mean, not the middle value, even after it skips the NULLs; NULLs don’t cause an error, because AVG simply leaves them out.
quiz.learning_outcome: Know who is in an average before you report it.

modules.title: SQL for real questions: joins and windows
modules.summary: Combine tables with joins, avoid double counting, and compare rows with window functions such as ROW_NUMBER and LAG.
modules.outcome: Combine tables with joins without double counting, and compare rows with window functions such as ROW_NUMBER and LAG.

learn.title: Joins connect facts to context
learn.body:
An orders table knows each customer_id. A customers table knows their city and sign-up date. A join connects them. INNER JOIN keeps only rows that match in both tables. LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table, and fills in NULL where nothing matches.

Worked example: customers A, B and C. A has 2 orders, B has 1 and C has none.
SELECT c.customer_id, o.order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id;
Result: 4 rows. A twice, B once, and C with order_id NULL. Add WHERE o.order_id IS NULL, and only C is left: a customer who never ordered.

Common trap: after a LEFT JOIN, a WHERE condition on an orders column, such as o.order_date >= '2026-04-01', drops C. NULL fails the test, so the LEFT JOIN quietly becomes an INNER JOIN. Put that condition in the ON clause instead.

learn.title: Watch the row count
learn.body:
A join can multiply rows. This is called fan-out.

Worked example: Ravi, a customer in Indore, has 3 orders of ₹500 each, ₹1,500 in all. He also has 2 saved addresses. Join orders to addresses on customer_id, and each order matches both addresses. You get 6 rows, and SUM(order_value) says ₹3,000. Revenue has doubled, but nothing more was sold.

Catch it by counting rows and a total before and after every join:
SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(order_value) FROM orders;
Run the same count on the joined result. If either number grows, the key is not unique on the other side.

Fix it by joining to a table with one row per key, or by summarising the other table first. Before any join, ask: one row per what?

learn.title: Window functions compare rows
learn.body:
GROUP BY squashes rows into groups. A window function keeps every row and adds context to it.
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date) numbers each customer’s orders.
Summary functions work as windows too: AVG(order_value) OVER (PARTITION BY city) puts each city’s average on every order row, so you can compare each order with it.
LAG(x) OVER (ORDER BY …) brings in the value from the row before. LEAD looks one row ahead.

Worked example: monthly revenue for a Nashik shop.
SELECT month, revenue, LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS last_month
FROM monthly;
Jan | ₹4.1 lakh | NULL
Feb | ₹4.6 lakh | ₹4.1 lakh
Mar | ₹4.3 lakh | ₹4.6 lakh
revenue - last_month is the change: +₹0.5 lakh in February, −₹0.3 lakh in March.

You can’t use a window function in WHERE. Work it out in a WITH step (a CTE) or a subquery first, then filter, for example WHERE rn = 1.

tasks.title: Find the silent customers
tasks.prompt: In shell.duckdb.org, load orders as in Module 4 (SQL foundations), and the customers table: CREATE TABLE customers AS SELECT * FROM 'https://myskills.org.in/practice-data/masala-mart/customers.csv'; It has customer_id, city, signed_up and channel. Write a query that lists customers who signed up in 2026 but have never ordered. Report how many there are, and paste your query.
tasks.hint: LEFT JOIN customers to orders, then keep the rows where the order side IS NULL. Check: run it again without the 2026 condition. That count must be bigger.

tasks.title: First order or repeat?
tasks.prompt: Use ROW_NUMBER to number each customer’s orders by date, across all their orders since October 2025. Then work out what share of April 2026 revenue came from repeat orders (row number 2 or more). Paste your query and the share, to one decimal place.
tasks.hint: Number the orders in a WITH step before you filter to April. If you filter April first, each customer’s first April order looks like a first order, and the share comes out far too small. Order by order_date, then order_id, so ties are numbered the same way every time.

reflection.prompt: Have you ever seen a number that was “too good to be true”? Could a join that duplicated rows have explained it?
reflection.hint: Doubled revenue is a classic sign.

quiz.title: Students who haven’t applied
quiz.scenario: A college placement cell has students(student_id, branch) and applications(student_id, company, applied_on). The placement officer wants every student who hasn’t applied to any company since 1 August 2026, including those who never applied.
quiz.question: Which query lists them?
options: SELECT s.student_id FROM students s LEFT JOIN applications a ON a.student_id = s.student_id WHERE a.applied_on >= '2026-08-01' AND a.student_id IS NULL;
SELECT s.student_id FROM students s INNER JOIN applications a ON a.student_id = s.student_id AND a.applied_on >= '2026-08-01' WHERE a.student_id IS NULL;
SELECT s.student_id FROM students s LEFT JOIN applications a ON a.student_id = s.student_id AND a.applied_on >= '2026-08-01' WHERE a.student_id IS NOT NULL;
SELECT s.student_id FROM students s LEFT JOIN applications a ON a.student_id = s.student_id AND a.applied_on >= '2026-08-01' WHERE a.student_id IS NULL;
quiz.explanation: The LEFT JOIN keeps every student. With the date test in ON, only applications from 1 August join. A student with none gets NULL on the applications side, and IS NULL keeps them.
quiz.why_wrong: With the date test in WHERE, rows whose applied_on is NULL fail it, so the students you want vanish and the query returns nothing; an INNER JOIN drops students with no matching application, so IS NULL finds nothing; IS NOT NULL keeps the students who did apply.
quiz.learning_outcome: After a LEFT JOIN, put conditions on the right-hand table in ON, not WHERE.

quiz.title: Revenue that grew overnight
quiz.scenario: An analyst joins orders (10,000 rows, ₹82 lakh revenue) to customer_addresses, where some customers have two or three saved addresses. The joined table shows ₹1.3 crore.
quiz.question: What most likely happened?
options: The join added orders for addresses that had no customer linked to them
Revenue was stored in rupees in one table and in paise in the other
Orders were repeated once for each matching address, inflating the total
Orders placed after the first query ran were included in the second
quiz.explanation: A one-to-many join repeats each order for every address its customer has, so summing order values double or triple counts.
quiz.why_wrong: A join can’t create orders that weren’t in the orders table; a unit mix-up would change every row by the same factor, not only some; the data didn’t change between the two queries.
quiz.learning_outcome: Check totals after a join to catch double counting.

quiz.title: Latest visit only
quiz.scenario: A physiotherapy centre in Kozhikode has a table visits(visit_id, patient_id, visit_date, therapist). You need one row per patient: their most recent visit.
quiz.question: Which expression, kept where it equals 1, picks each patient’s latest visit?
options: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY patient_id ORDER BY visit_date)
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY patient_id ORDER BY visit_date DESC)
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY patient_id, visit_date ORDER BY visit_date DESC)
RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY visit_date ORDER BY patient_id)
quiz.explanation: PARTITION BY patient_id restarts the numbering for each patient, and ORDER BY visit_date DESC puts the newest visit first. So row 1 is each patient’s latest visit.
quiz.why_wrong: Ascending order makes row 1 the first visit, not the latest; partitioning by patient and date restarts the count for every visit date, so nearly every row is 1; RANK partitioned by date ranks patients within each day, not visits within each patient.
quiz.learning_outcome: Choose the partition and the sort direction to pick one row per group.

quiz.title: Each order against its city
quiz.scenario: A Siliguri tea trader’s orders table has order_id, city and value. You need every order shown next to its city’s average order value, to flag unusually large orders.
quiz.question: Which approach puts each city’s own average next to every order?
options: AVG(value) OVER (ORDER BY city) alongside each order
SELECT DISTINCT city, AVG(value), then sort by the average
HAVING AVG(value) > value after a GROUP BY on city
AVG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY city) alongside each order
quiz.explanation: AVG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY city) works out the average inside each city and adds it to every order row, without collapsing the rows.
quiz.why_wrong: ORDER BY without PARTITION BY gives a running average that mixes in the cities before it, not each city’s own average; putting city next to AVG with no GROUP BY or OVER stops with an error in DuckDB, and even with GROUP BY it gives one row per city, not every order; HAVING filters groups and can’t compare each order with its group.
quiz.learning_outcome: Window functions add group context without losing detail.

modules.title: Statistics that change decisions
modules.summary: Variation, samples, bias and A/B tests: tell a real change from noise.
modules.outcome: Use spread, samples and a simple A/B test to tell a real change from noise.

learn.title: Variation is normal
learn.body:
Numbers move around even when nothing has changed: weekends, salary days, rain, festivals. These ordinary ups and downs are called noise.

Worked example: for the last 8 weeks, a Bhopal clinic saw 110 to 150 patients a day. The average was about 130. On Monday it saw 158. That is above the usual range, but only just, and only for one day. Before calling it a change, watch the next week. If most days stay above 150, something has changed. If they fall back to 110 to 150, Monday was noise.

Standard deviation measures how far a typical day is from the average. In Google Sheets, =STDEV(B2:B57) gives it for 56 days. A day more than about 2 standard deviations from the average is unusual. Check that before you celebrate or panic.

learn.title: Samples and who answered
learn.body:
A survey of 200 students is not every student. It is a sample. Its result has a range of error around it, called the margin of error.

Worked example: 72% of students who answered say they are satisfied.
- From 50 answers, the figure for all students could be anywhere from about 60% to 85%.
- From 2,000 answers, it is within about 2 points.
Bigger samples give narrower ranges.

Then ask who answered. Say a college emails a survey and only 1 in 10 students replies. The replies may come mostly from the happiest and the angriest students. This is called non-response bias.

A bigger sample does not fix bias. 5,000 replies from the wrong people still mislead. Ask how people were chosen before you trust the number.

learn.title: A/B tests answer “did it work?”
learn.body:
An A/B test splits people at random into two groups at the same time. Group A sees the old version and group B the new one. Random assignment balances everything else, such as city, phone and income. So a clear difference can be credited to the change.

Worked example: a Jaipur online tutor tests a new sign-up page. Before starting, she decides three things. The measure: paid sign-ups per visitor. The run: 2 full weeks, so both weekends count. The size: about 1,000 visitors per page.
Result: old page 40 of 1,000 (4.0%); new page 64 of 1,000 (6.4%).

Is a 2.4-point gap more than chance? A free online A/B test calculator compares the two groups. Here, a gap this big would rarely happen by chance alone.

The common mistake: checking every day and stopping the moment it “looks good”. Early gaps are often noise.

tasks.title: Design a test
tasks.prompt: An edtech app wants to know whether a ₹99 first-month offer brings more paid sign-ups than a 7-day free trial. Write a one-page A/B test plan under five headings. Who is in it? How are they split? What do you measure? How long does it run? What result would make you pick a winner?
tasks.hint: What could go wrong if the offer ran only in one city, or only in the first week? Decide the run length before you start.

tasks.title: Noise or signal?
tasks.prompt: A Coimbatore shop’s daily sales for the last 10 days, in ₹ thousand, were: 44, 41, 49, 38, 52, 46, 43, 47, 40, 45. Yesterday, after a new shelf layout, sales were ₹54,000. Put the 10 numbers in Google Sheets and find the average, the lowest, the highest and the standard deviation. Then write 3 or 4 sentences for the owner: is ₹54,000 unusual, and what would you check before saying the layout worked?
tasks.hint: Use =AVERAGE, =MIN, =MAX and =STDEV. How many standard deviations above the average is 54? Is one day enough to decide?

reflection.prompt: When have you seen a survey or “study” quoted that you now doubt? What would you want to know about how it was done?
reflection.hint: How many people, who were they, and who chose them?

quiz.title: Opt in, or random?
quiz.scenario: A Kanpur online pharmacy wants to test a new checkout page. A manager suggests showing it only to users who opt in, and comparing them with users who don’t.
quiz.question: Why should users be assigned to the two pages at random instead?
options: So the test finishes sooner, because nobody has to stop and choose which page to see
So both groups end up with exactly the same number of users every day
So users can’t pick a page, which would break the app’s terms of use
So the groups are alike except for the page, and a difference can be credited to it
quiz.explanation: Users who opt in may be keener or more used to the app, so they could buy more anyway. Random assignment spreads those differences evenly, so a gap between the groups comes from the page.
quiz.why_wrong: Random assignment doesn’t make a test faster; it gives groups of roughly equal size, not exactly equal every day; it is there to make the comparison fair, not to follow any terms of use.
quiz.learning_outcome: Random assignment is what makes a test fair.

quiz.title: Two app ratings
quiz.scenario: App A shows 4.9 stars from 40 reviews. App B shows 4.6 stars from 52,000 reviews.
quiz.question: Which statement is most defensible?
options: App A is clearly better, because its rating is higher and recent reviews matter more
Both are equally reliable, because a star rating is an average either way
App B’s rating is the more reliable estimate; App A’s could change a lot with more reviews
They can’t be compared at all, because the apps have different numbers of reviews
quiz.explanation: With 40 reviews a few new ones can move the average a lot; 52,000 reviews pin it down closely.
quiz.why_wrong: A higher average from 40 reviews can’t show A is better; reliability depends on how many ratings sit behind each average; the different review counts are exactly what tells you which to trust more.
quiz.learning_outcome: Small samples give uncertain results.

quiz.title: The early winner
quiz.scenario: A team checks its A/B test every hour, and stops it on day 2 because the new design is ahead by 9%.
quiz.question: What is the main risk?
options: Early leads swing by chance; stopping at the first good moment often crowns a false winner
None: a 9% lead after two days of traffic is enough to be confident the new design is better
Two days is too short for the servers to show both designs to a large enough number of users
Checking every hour slows the website down and changes how users behave
quiz.explanation: Results swing a lot early on. Checking constantly and stopping when ahead almost guarantees you’ll catch a lucky moment.
quiz.why_wrong: A two-day lead can be pure chance; showing two designs isn’t limited to a certain number of days; checking results doesn’t change what users see.
quiz.learning_outcome: Fix a test’s length before it starts.

quiz.title: The satisfied members
quiz.scenario: A gym chain surveys members who have just renewed, and 90% say they are “very satisfied”. The CEO wants “90% of our members are very satisfied” in an advert.
quiz.question: What is the problem?
options: 90% is too high to believe; honest satisfaction surveys of gym members rarely go above 70%
The survey needed more questions, about equipment and trainers, to measure satisfaction properly
Advertising rules allow survey results only when an outside agency ran the survey
Only members who renewed were asked; those who left are missing, so it overstates satisfaction
quiz.explanation: Asking only people who stayed leaves out those who left: a selection bias that flatters the result.
quiz.why_wrong: A high number can be true for the group asked; more questions don’t fix who was asked; the problem is the sample, not who ran the survey.
quiz.learning_outcome: Check who was left out of a sample.

modules.title: Python and pandas for analysis
modules.summary: Load, clean, filter, summarise and join data with pandas in a free Google Colab notebook, and check each step.
modules.outcome: Clean and summarise a real CSV file with pandas in a notebook, checking the row count and totals at each step.

learn.title: Why Python, and where to run it free
learn.body:
Python repeats your steps exactly on next month’s file. It handles millions of rows, and a notebook records every step so anyone can rerun it. pandas is Python’s table library. A DataFrame, usually called df, is a sheet you can program.

Run it free in Google Colab (colab.research.google.com) with a Google account. There is nothing to install. A laptop or a college computer is easier than a phone. Free sessions can stop when idle; if that happens, run the cells again from the top. Python in Excel also exists, but it needs a paid Microsoft 365 plan.

Worked example: your first cell.
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("https://myskills.org.in/practice-data/masala-mart/orders.csv")
df.shape
The output (2030, 9) means 2,030 rows and 9 columns. df.head() shows the first 5 rows, and df.info() shows each column’s type and blanks.

learn.title: From file to answer
learn.body:
A whole small analysis: a Hyderabad tiffin service’s file payments.csv has 4 rows:
txn_time,customer,amount,status
02/05/2026 08:10,R1,120,success
02/05/2026 13:05,R2,150,failed
03/05/2026 08:20,R1,120,success
05/05/2026 19:30,R2,150,success

df = pd.read_csv("payments.csv")
df["txn_time"] = pd.to_datetime(df["txn_time"], format="%d/%m/%Y %H:%M")
ok = df[df["status"] == "success"]
ok.groupby("customer")["amount"].sum()
Output: R1 240, R2 150.

Why format=? 02/05/2026 could be 2 May or 5 February. format= says exactly which, and stops with an error if a row doesn’t fit. dayfirst=True only prefers day-first; it is not strict.

The common mistake is letting pandas guess. Read month-first, 02/05/2026 becomes 5 February. Always look at a few converted dates with df.head() before you go on.

To bring in another table’s columns, merge on a shared key:
areas = pd.DataFrame({"customer": ["R1"], "area": ["Kondapur"]})
df = df.merge(areas, on="customer", how="left")
how="left" keeps every payment, like a LEFT JOIN. R2 has no match, so its area is NaN, pandas’ blank. Leave how= out and only matching rows stay.

learn.title: Filter, clean, then check
learn.body:
To filter on two conditions, use & for “and” and | for “or”. Put brackets round each condition:
df[(df["status"] == "success") & (df["amount"] > 5000)]
Python’s word and gives an error on whole columns, and so does leaving out the brackets.

To change values in matching rows, use df.loc[df["amount"] < 0, "status"] = "check". The older form df[df["amount"] < 0]["status"] = "check" never changes df in pandas 3 (January 2026). Colab may run an older pandas, so check pd.__version__.

To clean: df = df.drop_duplicates() removes rows identical in every column. subset="customer_id" compares only that column, so it would also delete every repeat order.
To turn “₹1,250” into a number:
df["order_value"] = df["order_value"].str.replace("₹", "").str.replace(",", "").astype(int)

After each step, compare df.shape and a total with the step before. If either grows after a merge, rows were duplicated, like a fan-out in SQL.

tasks.title: Clean and summarise the raw export
tasks.prompt: Open a new notebook in Google Colab and load the messy export: df = pd.read_csv("https://myskills.org.in/practice-data/masala-mart/orders_raw.csv"). Then: drop exact duplicate rows; turn order_date into dates with format="%d/%m/%Y"; turn order_value into numbers (remove "₹" and commas with .str.replace, then .astype(int)); merge in category from https://myskills.org.in/practice-data/masala-mart/products.csv with how="left". Finally, filter to kept orders (returned == 0) from April to June 2026, and total order_value by category, largest first. Report that table and df.shape after each step.
tasks.hint: Check yourself: after dropping duplicates you should have as many rows as orders.csv. After the merge, 58 rows have no category (new SKUs). If the filter gives an error, look for a missing bracket.

tasks.title: Read the code, then run it
tasks.prompt: Read this code and explain each line in plain words. df = pd.read_csv("https://myskills.org.in/practice-data/masala-mart/orders_raw.csv") / before = len(df) / df = df.drop_duplicates(subset="customer_id") / print(before - len(df)). Now run it. How many rows did it remove? Then reload the file and run df.drop_duplicates() with no subset instead. Which version removes only true duplicates? What would the other do to a revenue total?
tasks.hint: A customer who orders three times appears in three rows. Is that a duplicate?

reflection.prompt: What repetitive data task would you most like to automate? List the steps a script would follow.
reflection.hint: Anything you do every week in the same order is a candidate.

quiz.title: Totals by city
quiz.scenario: A Jalandhar sports-goods seller has loaded its orders into a DataFrame df with the columns order_id, city and value.
quiz.question: Which line gives the total order value for each city?
options: df.groupby("city")["value"].sum()
df.groupby("value")["city"].sum()
df["value"].sum() / df["city"].nunique()
df.pivot("city", "value").sum()
quiz.explanation: groupby makes one group per city; selecting "value" and summing gives each city’s total.
quiz.why_wrong: Grouping by value and summing city mixes up the two columns; total value divided by the number of cities is one average, not a total per city; this df.pivot call stops with an error and wouldn’t add anything up anyway.
quiz.learning_outcome: groupby plus an aggregate summarises by category.

quiz.title: The dairy’s monthly file
quiz.scenario: A Kolhapur dairy sends a delivery log every month. Its date column is written day first, such as 05/04/2026 for 5 April 2026. The owner wants the code to stop with an error if any row doesn’t follow that pattern, instead of guessing.
quiz.question: Which line should you use?
options: pd.to_datetime(df["date"], dayfirst=True)
pd.to_datetime(df["date"], format="%d/%m/%Y")
pd.to_datetime(df["date"], format="%m/%d/%Y")
pd.to_datetime(df["date"], errors="coerce")
quiz.explanation: format="%d/%m/%Y" says exactly how every date is written, so 05/04/2026 becomes 5 April. pandas stops with an error at any row that doesn’t fit.
quiz.why_wrong: dayfirst=True only prefers day first: if the first date is 04/13/2026, pandas can read every date month-first, with only a warning; %m/%d/%Y puts the month first, so 05/04/2026 becomes 4 May; errors="coerce" never stops, and quietly turns dates it can’t read into blanks (NaT).
quiz.learning_outcome: Give pandas the exact date format, so a bad row stops the code.

quiz.title: Orders with unknown customers
quiz.scenario: A Dhanbad electronics store runs orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="left"). A few orders have a customer_id that isn’t in customers.
quiz.question: What happens to those orders?
options: They are kept, with the customer columns empty (NaN)
They are dropped, because they have nothing to match in customers
The merge stops with an error naming the missing customer_ids
They are matched to the nearest customer_id that does exist
quiz.explanation: A left merge keeps every row of the left table; unmatched rows get NaN in the right table’s columns.
quiz.why_wrong: Dropping unmatched rows is what an inner merge does; pandas doesn’t raise an error for keys with no match; a merge only matches equal keys, never a “nearest” one.
quiz.learning_outcome: Choose the merge type for the rows you must keep.

quiz.title: Big successful payments
quiz.scenario: A Gwalior payment company has a DataFrame df of transactions, with status and amount columns.
quiz.question: Which line keeps only successful transactions above ₹5,000?
options: df[(df["status"] == "success") & (df["amount"] > 5000)]
df[(df["status"] == "success") and (df["amount"] > 5000)]
df[df["status"] == "success" & df["amount"] > 5000]
df[(df["status"] == "success") | (df["amount"] > 5000)]
quiz.explanation: pandas combines conditions on whole columns with & for “and”. Each condition needs its own brackets, so each comparison is worked out before & joins them.
quiz.why_wrong: Python’s word and can’t combine whole columns, so it raises an error; without brackets, & is applied first, to "success" and the amount column, which raises an error; | means “or”, so it would also keep failed transactions above ₹5,000.
quiz.learning_outcome: Combine pandas conditions with & and brackets.

modules.title: Dashboards people use
modules.summary: Choose the right chart, design a dashboard around decisions, build it with free tools, and check any number a tool drafts.
modules.outcome: Build a one-page dashboard that shows key numbers against targets, where the problem is, and what changed.

learn.title: Pick the chart for the question
learn.body:
Match the chart to the question.
- Change over time: a line chart.
- Comparing categories: a bar chart, sorted largest first.
- Part of a whole: a stacked bar, or a pie with only two or three slices.
- Two numbers together: a scatter plot.
- Exact values: a well-formatted table.

Common mistake: a bar chart whose axis doesn’t start at zero. Worked example: three stores sold ₹100 lakh, ₹101 lakh and ₹102 lakh. If the axis starts at ₹99 lakh, the bars are 1, 2 and 3 units tall. ₹102 lakh now looks three times ₹100 lakh, though it is only 2% more. Bars must start at zero.

A pie with nine slices is another trap. People can’t compare angles well, but a sorted bar chart shows the order at once.

learn.title: A dashboard answers three questions
learn.body:
A good dashboard page answers three questions, from top to bottom.
1. Are we on track? Key numbers against their targets.
2. Where is the problem? A breakdown by city, centre, channel or product.
3. What changed? A trend against earlier periods.

Worked example: a coaching chain with 6 centres in Nagpur, Indore and Raipur.
- Top row: admissions this month, 412 against a target of 450. Fees collected, ₹38 lakh against ₹40 lakh.
- Middle: a sorted bar chart of admissions by centre. Centres below target are red; the rest are grey.
- Bottom: a line chart of weekly admissions for the last 12 weeks.
The area head sees at once that 2 centres are behind, and calls them.

Put the most important number top left. Keep each page to one purpose. Use colour only to point at what needs action.

learn.title: Build it free
learn.body:
You can build a dashboard free in three ways.
- Looker Studio (lookerstudio.google.com): free in any browser. Connect it to a Google Sheet, then add scorecards, charts and filters. It is easiest on a laptop.
- Google Sheets charts: Insert > Chart. They work on a phone too, and are enough for a simple one-page view.
- Power BI Desktop: free on a Windows computer, and used by many employers in India. It has no Mac or phone version.

In Power BI you write measures in DAX, its formula language. For example:
Return rate = DIVIDE(SUM(Orders[returned]), COUNTROWS(Orders))
Every chart reuses the measure, so the number is the same everywhere.

Copilot in Power BI can draft measures and pages. It is a paid feature some employers provide. Whatever drafted a number, check it against a total you trust before you share it.

tasks.title: Build Masala Mart’s dashboard
tasks.prompt: Build a one-page dashboard for Masala Mart’s founder from orders.csv, loaded into a Google Sheet as in Module 2 (Spreadsheets that answer questions). Use Looker Studio connected to your Sheet, or Google Sheets charts; Power BI Desktop is fine if you have Windows. Include: three key numbers for September 2026 against their targets (revenue, target ₹85,000; orders, target 200; return rate, target under 5%); a sorted bar chart of revenue by city; and a line chart of monthly revenue from October 2025. Submit a link or a screenshot, and one sentence on what the founder should act on.
tasks.hint: Check your September revenue against a SUMIFS or pivot total before you share. Colour only the numbers that miss their target. Does the line chart show the Diwali season?

tasks.title: Fix a bad chart
tasks.prompt: A colleague shows Masala Mart’s revenue by city as a 3D pie with 10 slices. Make that pie yourself in Google Sheets from a pivot of revenue by city, then redraw it as a better chart. Which city is third, and how easy was that to see in each chart? Write two sentences on why your redraw is easier to read.
tasks.hint: Would a sorted bar chart say it more clearly? Check that its axis starts at zero.

reflection.prompt: Which number at your college, job or home would be worth tracking on a dashboard? What would you do differently if it went down?
reflection.hint: A good dashboard number leads to an action.

quiz.title: Is revenue rising?
quiz.scenario: A fertiliser dealer in Guntur has 18 months of revenue figures. The owner wants to see whether monthly revenue has risen, and whether it dips in the same months each year.
quiz.question: Which chart shows this best?
options: A line chart of revenue by month
A pie chart of revenue by month
A scatter plot of revenue by month
A bar chart sorted by revenue
quiz.explanation: Change over time is a line chart’s job. The months run left to right in order, so a rise, a fall or a yearly dip shows at once.
quiz.why_wrong: A pie shows parts of a whole and loses the order of the months; a scatter plot is for two measures that move together, and its separate dots make a trend harder to follow; sorting bars by revenue breaks the time order the owner needs.
quiz.learning_outcome: Use line charts for trends over time.

quiz.title: The giant jump
quiz.scenario: A Madurai jewellery chain’s bar chart shows this quarter’s sales at ₹52 lakh against ₹50 lakh last quarter. The new bar looks twice as tall as the old one.
quiz.question: What is most likely wrong?
options: The value axis starts near ₹48 lakh instead of zero, exaggerating a 4% rise
The data is wrong: a 4% rise can’t produce a bar that much taller
The bars are drawn in 3D, which makes the nearer bar look larger
The two quarters are measured in different units, so the bars can’t be compared directly
quiz.explanation: Readers judge bars by their length. With the axis starting at ₹48 lakh, the bars are 2 and 4 units tall, so a 4% rise looks like 100%. Bars must start at zero.
quiz.why_wrong: The numbers can be right while the drawing misleads; 3D can distort sizes a little, but it can’t double a bar; nothing suggests a units mix-up, and an axis starting at ₹48 lakh explains the doubling exactly.
quiz.learning_outcome: Start bar chart axes at zero.

quiz.title: The 30-minute promise
quiz.scenario: The operations head of a food-delivery company wants to see at a glance whether any city is missing its 30-minute delivery target.
quiz.question: What should the top of the dashboard show?
options: A table of every late order, so the head can read through the details
The national average delivery time, compared with last month
Total orders per city, since the busiest cities are the likeliest to be late
Each city’s on-time delivery % against the target, below-target cities highlighted
quiz.explanation: The question is “which city is off target?”, so the top shows that measure for each city with problems highlighted.
quiz.why_wrong: Every late order is too much detail; one national average hides which city is off target; busy cities aren’t necessarily the late ones.
quiz.learning_outcome: Design a dashboard around the decision it supports.

quiz.title: Two repeat rates
quiz.scenario: Copilot in Power BI drafts a measure, Repeat Customer Rate, that returns 74%. Your earlier SQL analysis found 41% for the same period.
quiz.question: What should you do first?
options: Publish Copilot’s figure, as it uses the live data model rather than an older query
Report both numbers side by side and let readers decide which to trust
Rerun your SQL until it matches Copilot, since the dashboard is what people see
Read the DAX it wrote, compare its definition and period with yours, then reconcile
quiz.explanation: Two methods disagreeing usually means two definitions. Reading the generated DAX shows what it actually calculates, so you can fix whichever is wrong.
quiz.why_wrong: Using the live model doesn’t make a definition right; two unexplained numbers confuse readers; forcing your SQL to match hides which definition is correct.
quiz.learning_outcome: Reconcile AI-drafted measures against a trusted result.

modules.title: AI as your analysis partner
modules.summary: Prompt free AI assistants well, check everything they produce against the data, and keep personal data safe.
modules.outcome: Use a free AI assistant to draft analysis, then check its output against the data before anyone relies on it.

learn.title: What AI is good at, and how to ask
learn.body:
AI assistants can draft SQL and pandas code from a plain-English question. They can explain a formula, suggest cleaning steps and propose charts. Free assistants such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini can all do this. Copilot in Excel and Power BI does too, on paid plans some employers provide.

They work best when you give them context. Worked example of a strong prompt:
“I use DuckDB. Table orders has order_id, order_date (a DATE), customer_id, order_value in ₹, and returned (1 or 0). Write a query for monthly revenue from kept orders (returned = 0) in 2026. One row per month, oldest first. Explain each line.”

It names the tool, the table, the columns, what they mean, and the output wanted. A weak prompt, “write SQL for monthly sales”, leaves the AI to guess all of that.

learn.title: Catch it before it costs you
learn.body:
AI can write code that runs but answers a different question. It can invent column names, mishandle dates or blanks, and state wrong numbers confidently. Treat its output like a new colleague’s first draft.

Worked example: a Kochi pharmacy asks for “monthly active customers”. The AI writes:
SELECT month, COUNT(customer_id) FROM orders GROUP BY month;
It runs. But COUNT(customer_id) counts orders, not people. You check 10 orders from one month by hand: 7 different customers placed them, but the query says 10. The fix:
SELECT month, COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) FROM orders GROUP BY month;

Three checks catch most mistakes.
1. Run it on a small sample you can count by hand.
2. Compare a total with a source you trust.
3. Read the code for the definition: what exactly is counted?
Asking the same AI “is this right?” is not a check.

learn.title: Protect people’s data
learn.body:
Don’t paste personal data into public AI tools. That includes names, phone numbers, Aadhaar numbers and health details.

India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 sets the rules. Personal data may be used only for a lawful purpose. That needs the person’s consent, or one of a few legitimate uses the Act lists. The data must also be kept safe. The DPDP Rules, 2025 bring in the duties in phases, and most apply to organisations from May 2027. Good practice starts now.

Worked example: you want AI help with a clinic’s appointments file. Use the tools your organisation approves. Otherwise, share only the column names and a made-up row:
patient_id, visit_date, department, fee
P001, 2026-05-02, ENT, 500
Then run the code the AI writes on the real data yourself.

tasks.title: Prompt, then check
tasks.prompt: Use any free AI assistant, such as ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini. Give it only the column names of Masala Mart’s orders.csv, not the data. Ask it for a DuckDB query that shows, for each month, the share of customers who were repeat customers. Define “repeat customer” in your prompt yourself. Run the query in shell.duckdb.org on orders.csv. Then run the three checks from the second card. Submit your prompt, the query, one month’s result, and what each check found.
tasks.hint: Decide first: is a repeat customer someone who ordered in an earlier month, or someone with 2 or more orders this month? The two give very different numbers.

tasks.title: Catch the error
tasks.prompt: An AI assistant read Masala Mart’s orders.csv and wrote: “Revenue grew 60% from Q1 to Q2 2026, driven by Bengaluru.” Check both parts against the data with a pivot table or SUMIFS in Google Sheets. Q1 is January to March and Q2 is April to June. Find the mistake, work out what the AI most likely did wrong, and rewrite the sentence correctly.
tasks.hint: Recalculate both quarters from the rows yourself. If your growth figure differs, try other date ranges to see which one gives 60%.

reflection.prompt: Where would you trust an AI assistant fully, and where would you always check its work? Why the difference?
reflection.hint: Think about the cost of a mistake in each case.

quiz.title: Average fare per route
quiz.scenario: A bus-booking app keeps its data in DuckDB, in a table bookings(booking_id, user_id, route, booked_at, fare). The operations head wants the average fare on each route for October 2026.
quiz.question: Which prompt is most likely to get correct SQL from an AI assistant?
options: “Write SQL for the average fares on my bus booking app last month. Make it efficient and easy to read.”
“DuckDB. Table bookings(booking_id, user_id, route, booked_at, fare): average fare per route, October 2026, highest first.”
“You are an expert data analyst with 20 years of experience. Analyse my bus booking data and tell me everything about fares.”
“Using my company database, work out the average fare for each route last month and draw it as a bar chart.”
quiz.explanation: It names the tool, the table and its columns, the measure, the period and the order of the output. The assistant has nothing to guess.
quiz.why_wrong: “Make it efficient” gives no table, columns or exact period, so the assistant must invent them; the expert persona names neither the table nor the measure; “my company database” gives the assistant no schema to work from.
quiz.learning_outcome: Give AI the schema, the definition and the goal.

quiz.title: Code that runs
quiz.scenario: AI-written pandas code runs without errors and reports an average order value of ₹1,240.
quiz.question: What is the best way to check it?
options: Work out the same figure another way for a month you know, such as with a PivotTable
Trust it: code that runs on the full file without errors has been checked by Python
Ask the assistant to double-check its own code and confirm the figure
Compare it with last year’s average order value; if it’s close, it’s right
quiz.explanation: An independent calculation is the only real check: code can run perfectly and still compute the wrong thing.
quiz.why_wrong: Running without errors says nothing about correctness; the assistant checking itself isn’t independent; last year’s figure can’t confirm this year’s calculation.
quiz.learning_outcome: Verify AI output with an independent calculation.

quiz.title: The patient list
quiz.scenario: You want an AI assistant’s help cleaning a list of 20,000 patients with names, phone numbers and diagnoses.
quiz.question: What is the right approach?
options: Paste the whole file into a free AI chatbot, since it deletes conversations once you close the window
Remove the diagnosis column first, then share the names and phone numbers, which aren’t sensitive
Use an approved tool, or share only the column names and made-up rows and run the code yourself
Replace names with initials, keep the phones and diagnoses, and paste it into a free chatbot
quiz.explanation: Personal and health data must stay within approved systems. Sharing the structure with made-up rows gets the help without exposing anyone.
quiz.why_wrong: You can’t be sure a free chatbot doesn’t keep what you paste; names and phone numbers are personal data on their own; initials don’t hide anyone while phone numbers and diagnoses stay.
quiz.learning_outcome: Never share personal data with unapproved AI tools.

quiz.title: The column that isn’t there
quiz.scenario: AI-written SQL refers to a column customers.lifetime_value, which doesn’t exist in your database.
quiz.question: What does this tell you?
options: The database is missing a column the query needs, so ask IT to add lifetime_value to the table
It guessed your schema: give it the real table definitions and re-check the whole query
Create the column and fill it with sample values so the query can run
Remove that line; if the rest of the query runs, its result can be trusted
quiz.explanation: An invented column shows the assistant was guessing, so other parts may be guesses too. Supply the schema and re-check everything.
quiz.why_wrong: lifetime_value was invented, not missing; filling it with made-up values corrupts the result; a query that runs can still be wrong.
quiz.learning_outcome: An invented detail means: re-check the whole answer.

modules.title: From numbers to decisions
modules.summary: Lead with the recommendation, turn findings into actions, and be honest about limits.
modules.outcome: Write a recommendation a manager can act on from its first two lines, with the evidence and its honest limits.

learn.title: Lead with the answer
learn.body:
Most managers read the first two lines, then decide whether to read on. So start with the recommendation and the number behind it.

Before: “This report analyses six months of marketing data from January to June 2026 across two channels.”
After: “Move ₹2 lakh a month from Meta ads to Google Search in Pune. Search brings in a customer for ₹310, against ₹780 on Meta.”

What changed? The action comes first. It names the amount, the place and the channel. The one number that justifies it comes next. After that come the evidence and then the limits.

The common mistake is telling the story of your work in the order you did it. The manager needs the decision, not your journey.

learn.title: So what, and now what?
learn.body:
For every chart, say what it shows and what it means for the decision. A finding says what the data shows. An insight says why it matters. An action says what to do next.

Worked example from a Nagpur bookshop:
- Finding: weekend sales are 40% of the week’s sales, but the same 2 staff work every day.
- Insight: at weekends customers wait at the counter, and some leave without buying.
- Action: add a part-time staff member at weekends for a month. Then compare weekend sales with last month.

The action is small, specific and testable. “Improve the weekend experience” is not an action, because nobody knows what to do on Monday.

Write job titles and terms in full the first time: finance head (CFO), cash on delivery (COD).

learn.title: Be honest about uncertainty
learn.body:
State the period, the data source, the sample size and what you couldn’t check. A recommendation with clear limits earns more trust than a confident one that later falls apart.

Worked example: a one-line caveat under a skincare brand’s recommendation.
“Based on 14,000 customers, January to June 2026. Customers chose the trial kit themselves, so keen buyers may have picked it. A 4-week A/B test would confirm it.”

That line does three jobs. It says how much data there is. It names the main doubt: people chose for themselves (you met this in the first module and the statistics module). And it says what would settle the doubt.

The common mistake is hiding limits in a footnote, or leaving them out. If your manager finds a limit you didn’t mention, they stop trusting the rest.

tasks.title: Write the memo opening
