tasks.prompt: In Module 2 (Spreadsheets that answer questions) you found Masala Mart’s return rate by payment method (orders.csv, October 2025 to September 2026). Cash on delivery (COD) orders are returned far more often than UPI or card orders. Assume each return costs the brand about ₹90 in shipping both ways. Write the first paragraph of a memo to the founder: your recommendation first, the numbers behind it, and one honest caveat.
tasks.hint: Recommendation first, evidence second, one caveat. Did customers choose how to pay? What would a test show?

tasks.title: Turn findings into actions
tasks.prompt: Three findings from a college canteen’s sales data: 60% of sales happen between 12:30 and 1:30 pm; the queue takes 14 minutes at peak; 30% of students who arrive at peak leave without buying. Write one insight and one action for each finding.
tasks.hint: What could the canteen change by next week? Make each action small enough to test.

reflection.prompt: Think of a presentation or message that persuaded you. What did the person do that you could use in your own reports?
reflection.hint: Notice what came first, and what they left out.

quiz.title: Two minutes with the operations head
quiz.scenario: You analysed a year of returns for an Agra footwear brand that sells online. The operations head has two minutes before a meeting and will read only your first line.
quiz.question: Which opening line should you send?
options: “Recommendation: offer free size exchanges instead of refunds; size returns cost us about ₹4 lakh a month.”
“This report analyses 14 tables and 2.1 million rows from our order, return and payment systems.”
“Data was collected from several sources over twelve months and cleaned with a documented process.”
“Here are 25 charts covering sales, returns, exchanges and payments, organised by region, by store and by month.”
quiz.explanation: It leads with an action and the money behind it, so the head can decide in the two minutes available. The evidence and the limits can follow.
quiz.why_wrong: The count of tables and rows says how big the work was, not what to do; how the data was collected is method, which belongs lower down; 25 charts leave the reader to find the point alone.
quiz.learning_outcome: Lead with the recommendation and its impact.

quiz.title: The weekly update
quiz.scenario: An analyst at a Mysuru online furniture store drafts four lines for the weekly update to the founder.
quiz.question: Which line is an insight with an action, not just a finding?
options: “The average order value is ₹6,400, slightly higher than in the same month last year.”
“40% of carts are dropped at the delivery fee; show it on product pages for a month and compare.”
“We now have 12,000 customers, most in Maharashtra and Karnataka, up from 9,000 last year.”
“Sales were higher in October, when the festive season began across the country.”
quiz.explanation: It links a specific problem, carts dropped at the delivery fee, to a likely cause. It also names a small change and a way to test it.
quiz.why_wrong: ₹6,400 against last year is a finding with no “so what”; the customer count by state is growth with no action attached; linking October sales to the festive season explains a finding but says nothing to do next.
quiz.learning_outcome: Turn findings into insights by adding “so what” and “now what”.

quiz.title: Festive data
quiz.scenario: Your analysis of a jewellery brand’s website rests on three weeks of data, all during Diwali.
quiz.question: What should your memo say about it?
options: Nothing: mentioning limits would make the reader doubt the whole analysis
That the results are certain, because the festive weeks have the most orders of the whole year
That it covers only three festive weeks, which may not reflect a normal month, so re-check it
Remove the festive weeks, and say there isn’t yet enough normal-month data to report anything
quiz.explanation: Saying what the data covers, and when to check again, lets the reader act sensibly on the result.
quiz.why_wrong: Hiding a limit misleads; festive weeks aren’t typical of the rest of the year; withholding the results helps no one.
quiz.learning_outcome: State the limits of your data and how to address them.

quiz.title: Did the loyalty programme pay?
quiz.scenario: The chief financial officer (CFO) of a Pune supermarket chain asks whether the loyalty programme it launched six months ago has paid for itself.
quiz.question: Which answer is most useful?
options: “Yes: engagement is up across app opens, product reviews and referrals in the six months since the launch.”
“Yes: members spent ₹38 lakh more than shoppers who aren’t members over six months, so it has clearly paid off.”
“Yes: members spent ₹38 lakh more than similar shoppers who didn’t join; it cost ₹22 lakh, so ₹16 lakh net.”
“It’s too early to say; loyalty programmes usually take a year to show results.”
quiz.explanation: It answers in money, subtracts the cost, and compares members with similar shoppers who didn’t join, because keen shoppers spent more even before they joined.
quiz.why_wrong: Engagement doesn’t answer a money question; comparing members with all non-members ignores that keen shoppers already spent more, and leaves out the cost; six months of data can already answer it.
quiz.learning_outcome: Answer the question asked, in its own terms.

questions.title: Is marketing working?
questions.scenario: Hamsa runs marketing for a Bhubaneswar snack brand that sells online. From April to June she spent ₹6 lakh on Instagram ads and ₹6 lakh on Google ads. She asks you, “Is our marketing working?” She must set next quarter’s budget by Friday.
questions.question: Which version of her question can an analysis actually answer?
options: “Did Q2 Instagram customers cost less per first order than Google ones, and should budget move?”
“Are our Instagram and Google campaigns working, judging by the likes, clicks and reach they got in Q2?”
“What are all our marketing numbers for the last year, by channel and by month?”
“Do customers like our ads, and which of them do they remember best?”
questions.explanation: It names the channels, the period (Q2), one measure (cost per first order) and the decision it feeds (moving budget). So the data can answer it before Friday.
questions.why_wrong: Likes, clicks and reach measure attention, not whether the ads bring paying customers; every number by month answers no particular question; whether customers like or remember ads needs a survey and points to no decision.
questions.learning_outcome: A question becomes answerable when it names a measure, a period and a decision.

questions.title: The red stores
questions.scenario: A Tiruchirappalli grocery chain’s dashboard turns a store red on any day its sales fall below ₹68,000. Store 12’s daily sales have been between ₹60,000 and ₹80,000 for 60 days. So it turns red on many ordinary days, and managers now ignore the colour.
questions.question: Which change would make the red flag most useful?
options: Flag a store when its 7-day average falls below its own usual range, not on one low day
Lower the red line to ₹55,000 for every store, so that the flag appears much less often
Drop the colour and show every store’s daily sales in a table, so managers judge for themselves
Turn a store red whenever today’s sales are below yesterday’s, to catch every drop early
questions.explanation: Store 12’s sales normally swing between ₹60,000 and ₹80,000, so one low day is noise. Comparing a 7-day average with the store’s own usual range flags a real fall and keeps red meaningful.
questions.why_wrong: One line for every store ignores each store’s own normal level, so a big store could fall a long way before turning red; a table removes the at-a-glance signal the dashboard exists for; comparing with yesterday turns ordinary daily swings red even more often.
questions.learning_outcome: Set alerts against normal variation, not single values.

questions.title: The SKUs that won’t match
questions.scenario: A Vijayawada wholesaler copies SKUs from suppliers’ PDF invoices into a sheet. It uses =XLOOKUP(B2, Master[SKU], Master[Category], "New SKU"). 300 of 4,000 lines show “New SKU”, but when you search the master by eye, those SKUs are there.
questions.question: What is the most likely cause?
options: The master isn’t sorted A to Z, and XLOOKUP needs sorted data to find an exact match
Some copied SKUs carry hidden spaces, so they aren’t exactly equal to the master’s
XLOOKUP is doing an approximate match, because the fourth argument wasn’t set to exact
Those 300 SKUs really are new, so add them to the master and run the lookup again
questions.explanation: A lookup matches only identical values. A SKU copied with a space before or after it looks the same on screen but doesn’t match. Trim the column, then check that the count of “New SKU” falls.
questions.why_wrong: XLOOKUP’s exact match works on unsorted data; its fourth argument is the not-found value, and its default match is already exact; the SKUs are already in the master, so adding them again creates duplicates and leaves the real cause in place.
questions.learning_outcome: When a lookup fails on values that look equal, check for hidden spaces.

questions.title: The AI’s cleaning step
questions.scenario: A Shillong music school has 9,400 trial-class sign-ups (student_name, phone, instrument, signup_date). An AI assistant suggests df = df.drop_duplicates(subset="student_name") to remove repeat sign-ups. After it runs, 7,100 rows are left.
questions.question: What should you do before keeping the result?
options: Look at some removed rows: students can share a name, so match on name and phone
Keep it, because the code ran without errors and repeat sign-ups are very common
Ask the assistant whether 7,100 is the right count, and keep it if it agrees
Run drop_duplicates() with no subset instead, so it catches every repeated sign-up
questions.explanation: Dropping duplicates on name alone treats every student with the same name as one person, so real students disappear. Looking at the removed rows shows the problem, and matching on name and phone together keeps different people apart.
questions.why_wrong: Code that runs can still remove the wrong rows; the assistant checking its own number isn’t an independent check; with no subset, only rows identical in every column go, so repeat sign-ups on different dates stay.
questions.learning_outcome: Check what an AI-written cleaning step removed before you trust it.

questions.title: The income question
questions.scenario: An NGO in Ranchi surveys 800 households about their monthly income. 240 of them (30%) leave the income question blank. You are asked to report the average income.
questions.question: What is the best practice?
options: Fill the blanks with 0, so that every respondent is included in the average income
Fill each blank with the average of those who answered, so the sample size isn’t reduced
Report the average for those who answered, the share missing, and whether skippers differ
Report the average of those who answered, without mentioning the blanks
questions.explanation: A blank is unknown, not zero. Saying who is included, how many are missing, and whether the households that skipped look different keeps the average honest.
questions.why_wrong: Filling blanks with 0 invents zero incomes and drags the average down; filling with the average hides the gap and makes the result look more certain than it is; staying silent about 30% missing hides a limit the reader needs.
questions.learning_outcome: Report who is missing from an average, and whether they differ.

questions.title: Big payments by method
questions.scenario: A bill-payment app in Visakhapatnam keeps a payments table with payment_id, method (UPI, card or net banking) and amount in ₹. An analyst runs: SELECT method, COUNT(*) FROM payments WHERE amount > 1000 GROUP BY method;
questions.question: What does the result show?
options: The total amount paid above ₹1,000, for each payment method
The payment methods that have more than 1,000 payments
The average payment for each method, for payments over ₹1,000
The number of payments above ₹1,000 for each method
questions.explanation: WHERE keeps only payments above ₹1,000. GROUP BY method then makes one group per method, and COUNT(*) counts the payments in each.
questions.why_wrong: COUNT(*) counts payments, it doesn’t add their amounts; the 1,000 filters each payment’s amount, not the number of payments; COUNT gives a count, not an average.
questions.learning_outcome: Read WHERE as a row filter and COUNT(*) as a count per group.

questions.title: The pivot table that won’t add up
questions.scenario: A Tiruppur garment wholesaler pastes 6,000 order lines into Google Sheets and builds a pivot table of order_value by city. It shows a count of order_value, and switching to SUM gives 0 for every city. The order_value column holds entries like “Rs 1,250/-” and “Rs 980/-”.
questions.question: What should you do so the pivot table shows each city’s total?
options: Change the pivot table’s summary from SUM to AVERAGE, which works on text and numbers alike
Format the order_value column as Currency (₹), so the sheet reads it as money
Convert order_value to numbers (remove Rs, commas and /-), then refresh the pivot table
Add order_value to Rows as well as Values, so each amount is shown separately
questions.explanation: SUM skips text, and “Rs 1,250/-” is text, not a number. Once the column holds real numbers, the pivot table can add it up for each city.
questions.why_wrong: AVERAGE skips text too, so it fails in the same way; a currency format changes how a number looks but doesn’t turn text into a number; putting the amount in Rows lists each value instead of totalling it.
questions.learning_outcome: A pivot table can only add a column stored as numbers.

questions.title: Months when orders fell
questions.scenario: A quick-commerce dark store in Navi Mumbai keeps a table monthly_orders(month, orders), with one row per month. The manager wants the months in which orders fell compared with the month before.
questions.question: Which query lists those months?
options: WITH m AS (SELECT month, orders, LAG(orders) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev FROM monthly_orders) SELECT month FROM m WHERE orders < prev;
SELECT month FROM monthly_orders WHERE orders < LAG(orders) OVER (ORDER BY month);
WITH m AS (SELECT month, orders, LEAD(orders) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev FROM monthly_orders) SELECT month FROM m WHERE orders < prev;
WITH m AS (SELECT month, orders, LAG(orders) OVER (PARTITION BY month ORDER BY month) AS prev FROM monthly_orders) SELECT month FROM m WHERE orders < prev;
questions.explanation: LAG(orders) OVER (ORDER BY month) puts the previous month’s orders on each row. A window function can’t go in WHERE. So the WITH step works it out first, and the outer query keeps the months where orders < prev.
questions.why_wrong: A window function in WHERE stops with an error, because WHERE runs before windows are worked out; LEAD brings in the next month, so the query lists the months just before a rise, not the months that fell; PARTITION BY month makes each month its own window, so prev is always NULL and no month is listed.
questions.learning_outcome: Use LAG in a WITH step, then filter, to compare each period with the one before.

questions.title: Two figures for spending
questions.scenario: A survey of 2,000 households in Anand district, Gujarat, finds median monthly spending of ₹18,000 and mean spending of ₹31,000.
questions.question: What does the gap between the two figures suggest?
options: Spending is spread evenly, and most households spend about ₹31,000
The data must contain errors, since the median and the mean should be close
Most households spend more than ₹31,000, and a few spend very little
A few households with very high spending pull the mean above the median
questions.explanation: When the mean is far above the median, a small number of large values is pulling it up. Half the households spend ₹18,000 or less, so ₹31,000 isn’t typical.
questions.why_wrong: Even spending would put the mean and the median close together; a gap between them is normal when a few values are very large, not a sign of errors; if most households spent more than ₹31,000, the median would be above ₹31,000.
questions.learning_outcome: A mean well above the median signals a few very large values.

questions.title: A 0.1-point lead
questions.scenario: A train-ticket app is testing a new booking button. So far, version A converts 4.0% of 50,000 visitors and version B converts 4.1% of 50,000. The test has run 5 of its planned 14 days.
questions.question: What should you do before calling B the winner?
options: Declare B the winner, since 50,000 visitors per version is plenty of data for a clear result
Run the test again in a single city, to see whether B wins there too
Check the gap against chance with an A/B test calculator, and run all 14 days
Add a third version, C, to see whether the gap between them grows
questions.explanation: 4.0% and 4.1% of 50,000 are 2,000 and 2,050 conversions, a gap well within chance. An A/B test calculator would show this, and stopping on day 5 risks crowning a lucky early lead.
questions.why_wrong: A large sample can still show a gap that chance explains, and 0.1 points is tiny; one city shrinks the sample and makes chance bigger; adding version C changes the test without checking A against B.
questions.learning_outcome: A small gap needs checking against chance, over the planned run, before you name a winner.

questions.title: The checkout test, city by city
questions.scenario: A D2C brand tested a new checkout for its planned 3 weeks, with 120,000 visitors in each group. Conversion rose from 3.0% to 3.6%, far beyond normal variation. In Tier-3 cities alone (3,000 visitors per group), conversion fell from 2.8% to 2.5%.
questions.question: What should your memo recommend?
options: Roll it out only in metro and Tier-2 cities, since the Tier-3 result proves it fails there
Roll it out, and keep watching Tier-3 cities: 3,000 visitors a group is too few to judge
Hold the roll-out everywhere until Tier-3 cities also show a rise, so that no group loses out
Roll it out everywhere, and report a 20% rise in conversion for every city, Tier-3 included
questions.explanation: Across 120,000 visitors a group, 3.0% to 3.6% is far beyond chance, and the test ran its planned length. In Tier-3 cities the fall is 84 against 75 sales out of 3,000 each, well within chance. So roll out, and keep watching there.
questions.why_wrong: 9 sales out of 3,000 a group can’t prove the design fails in Tier-3 cities; holding everyone back gives up a clear, tested gain because of a result that may be chance; the 20% rise is for all visitors together, and Tier-3 cities didn’t show it.
questions.learning_outcome: Act on the overall result, and treat a small subgroup’s result as uncertain.

questions.title: Rows that multiplied
questions.scenario: A Nellore kitchenware seller has an orders table with 10,000 rows, one per order, and an order_total column. Its items table has one row per item in an order. An analyst runs df = orders.merge(items, on="order_id"), and the row count rises from 10,000 to 26,000.
questions.question: Why did the row count rise?
options: pandas added a blank row for every item with no matching order
The merge kept orders from both tables, including ones only in items
Each order matches several items, so each order repeats once per item
Some order IDs were read as text and others as numbers, so they doubled
questions.explanation: Each order matches every one of its items, so it appears once per item. Summing order_total on the merged table would now count each order several times.
questions.why_wrong: A merge without how= is an inner merge, so it never adds blank rows; keeping rows found only in items needs an outer merge; text and number keys make pandas stop with an error, not double the rows.
questions.learning_outcome: A one-to-many merge repeats each order once per matching item.

questions.title: Eleven tea brands
questions.scenario: A marketing intern must show the market share of 11 tea brands in Assam on one slide. The team wants to see which brands lead and how they rank.
questions.question: Which chart is clearest?
options: A pie chart with 11 slices, each labelled with its share
A horizontal bar chart, sorted largest first
A line chart of share by brand
A 3D pie chart with a legend
questions.explanation: Bars of different lengths are easy to compare, and sorting them puts the brands in rank order. Eleven pie slices are hard to compare by angle.
questions.why_wrong: Eleven slices are hard to compare by angle; a line suggests an order between brands that doesn’t exist; 3D distorts slice sizes, and a legend makes readers look back and forth.
questions.learning_outcome: Use a sorted bar chart to compare many categories.

questions.title: The 12% churn figure
questions.scenario: Your employer gives you an approved AI assistant. You ask it about a meal-kit company’s subscription sheet. It replies, “Your churn rate (the share of subscribers who cancelled) is 12%,” but doesn’t show how it worked that out. The figure is going into a board report.
questions.question: What should you do?
options: Use it, since AI tools calculate rates more reliably than spreadsheets do
Ask how it was calculated (definition, period, data), reproduce it, then use it
Ask the assistant to confirm it, and use it if it gives the same number again
Round it down to 10% to be safe, and note that it came from AI
questions.explanation: A number without a method can’t be trusted or explained. Asking for the definition, period and data, then reproducing the figure yourself, checks it before the board sees it.
questions.why_wrong: AI tools can calculate wrongly or use a different definition; asking again checks that it repeats itself, not that it is right; rounding down a number you can’t explain doesn’t make it safe.
questions.learning_outcome: Reproduce an AI’s figure before you use it.

questions.title: The memo’s first line
questions.scenario: A Tamil Nadu clinic chain ran a randomised test in 8 of its 30 clinics, covering 4,200 appointments over 6 weeks. SMS reminders sent the day before cut missed appointments from 18% to 11%. An AI assistant drafted four opening lines for your memo to the operations head.
questions.question: Which opening line should you use?
options: “SMS reminders end missed appointments for good, as our six-week test across the whole chain of clinics clearly proved.”
“We ran a 6-week randomised test in 8 clinics, covering 4,200 appointments; the method is described below.”
“Recommendation: send day-before SMS reminders in all 30 clinics; in an 8-clinic test, no-shows fell from 18% to 11%.”
“Recommendation: send SMS reminders in every clinic; patients prefer them, and the test was a big success.”
questions.explanation: It leads with a decision the reader can act on and the number behind it. It also describes the evidence exactly: a test in 8 clinics, not proof for the whole chain.
questions.why_wrong: “End” and “across the whole chain” overstate a test that cut no-shows to 11% in 8 clinics; starting with the method makes the reader hunt for the answer; nobody measured whether patients prefer SMS, and “a big success” replaces the number.
questions.learning_outcome: Choose the opening that leads with the action and states the evidence exactly.

project.brief:
Analyse 12 months of data for a real or realistic Indian business (for example a D2C brand, a café chain, a clinic or a coaching centre) and recommend one change that would grow revenue or cut costs.
Your mentor helps you choose the business, the question and a dataset: a public dataset (for example from data.gov.in), or data a business shares with you. If a business shares data, get its written permission. Remove names, phone numbers and other personal details before you analyse it, and never paste personal data into an AI tool.
Plan for about 20 hours over 3 to 4 weeks, with regular check-ins with your mentor. Every step can be done with free tools: Google Sheets, DuckDB in the browser, Google Colab and Looker Studio.
deliverables: A one-page problem statement: the decision, who makes it, and how success will be measured
The cleaned dataset, with a short data dictionary and a cleaning log (each step and the rows it changed)
Your SQL queries or Python notebook, with comments explaining each step
A one-page dashboard (Looker Studio, Google Sheets or Power BI) built around the decision
A one-page recommendation memo with honest limits and how you know the pattern is more than noise, and a 3-minute recorded walkthrough
An AI log: each prompt you used, what the AI produced, how you checked it and what you changed (or "no AI used")

rubric.description: Built around the decision: key numbers against target, honest axes, readable at a glance

rubric.description: Leads with the decision and its ₹ impact, states its limits, and the learner can explain every step
